newsitem.title: USA: Lilly recasts its pharmacy benefits unit.
newsitem.headline: Lilly recasts its pharmacy benefits unit.

text.p: Struggling to recover its investment, Eli Lilly and Co is recasting the mission of its PCS Health Systems after failing to turn the unit into a fast-track distribution channel for drug sales.
But industry analysts are skeptical Lilly will quickly recover its multi-billion dollar investment with PCS positioned as a broad-based health care information and management firm.

Lilly paid McKesson Corp $4.1 billion in November 1994 amid a wave of similar high-priced acquisitions of pharmacy benefit management companies that included buys by Merck and Co Inc and SmithKline Beecham Plc.

But the original aim of boosting drug sales by having the benefit manager influence doctors and patients to use more Lilly products has been stymied by federal regulators and managed care organizations, analysts said.

While Lilly has said PCS will continue to dilute Lilly profits at least through this year, a spokesman said the value of the unit should grow as its new programs gain acceptance in the marketplace. "PCS is going to be continue to be a very important element of our overall strategy as a company," the spokesman said.

In an bid to boost its value and spur future growth, last week Scottsdale, Ariz.-based PCS unveiled what it is calling its new identity as an "information-driven health solutions company," a transformation from its original position as a straight prescription processing firm.

"If we were to have stayed with the old paradigm, we would have lived with the risk of being faced with competitive forces in a quasi-commoditized market," PCS chief executive Jean-Pierre Millon said.

PCS executives said the company has invested heavily in the past 18 months to establish a computer network that will allow it to track drug prescription trends and provide information on patients and drugs to doctors and pharmacies.
"Turned around or not, it will take a long time for PCS to have a positive impact on Lilly," said ABB pharmaceutical industry analyst David Maris.

The unit's aim is to allow PCS customers, including managed care organizations, insurers and employers, to hold down healthcare costs while boosting use of a preferred list of drugs deemed most-cost-effective for a variety of conditions. There are four Lilly drugs on PCS's preferred list, or formulary, of 93 drugs. These are the diabetes treatments Humulin and Iletin, the anti-depressant Prozac and the ulcer medication Axid.

PCS executives said that, since the beginning of the year, the use by PCS clients of the list's 93 drugs, as opposed to other drugs, has risen to 50 percent from 45 percent. "With the trend line, a clear increase is continuing," said Jeff Sanders PCS vice president of marketing development.
Lilly could see more benefit from PCS as it brings to market drugs for chronic conditions, including one it is developing for osteoporosis, analysts said.
About 56 million people are covered by PCS, up from about 52 million at the time of its acquisition by Lilly, the executives said.
Analysts said Lilly might also seek one or more partners to share the costs of the PCS operation, but it is unlikely to unload PCS completely.

"It's premature to write PCS off," said James Keeney at Rodman and Renshaw. He estimated the unit's 1996 revenues at $392 million, up from $258 million in 1995. Lilly had $6.8 billion in total 1995 revenues.
